title: Lines, Angles, and Triangles
subtitle: Master angle relationships, congruence, similarity, and triangle properties

sections.title: Core Angle Rules
sections.content:
**Straight line:** angles on one side sum to $180°$
**Full rotation:** angles around a point sum to $360°$
**Vertical angles:** opposite angles formed by two intersecting lines are equal
**Supplementary:** two angles that sum to $180°$
**Complementary:** two angles that sum to $90°$

sections.title: Type 1: Parallel Lines Cut by a Transversal
The Angle Pairs
sections.content:
When a **transversal** cuts two parallel lines, it creates 8 angles. The key relationships:

- **Corresponding angles:** same position at each intersection → **equal**
- **Alternate interior angles:** between the parallel lines, on opposite sides → **equal**
- **Alternate exterior angles:** outside the parallel lines, on opposite sides → **equal**
- **Co-interior (same-side interior) angles:** between the lines, on the same side → **supplementary** (sum to $180°$)

**Quick rule:** If the angles look like they're in the same position (Z-shape, F-shape), they're equal. If they're on the same side and inside, they're supplementary.

sections.title: Example: Alternate Interior Angles
sections.problem: Line $t$ intersects parallel lines $m$ and $n$. At line $m$, the bottom-left angle is $170°$. What is the corresponding angle at line $n$?

steps.description: Corresponding angles (same position) are equal when lines are parallel

sections.title: Example: Find a Missing Angle with Parallel Lines
sections.problem: Two parallel lines $q$ and $r$ are cut by transversal $s$. At line $q$, the top-right angle is $58°$. What is the measure of the co-interior angle at line $r$ on the same side?

sections.title: Corresponding Parts Are Equal
sections.content:
When two triangles are **congruent**, all corresponding sides and angles are equal.

If $\triangle EFG \cong \triangle JKL$ (E↔J, F↔K, G↔L), then:
- $\angle E = \angle J$, $\angle F = \angle K$, $\angle G = \angle L$
- $EF = JK$, $FG = KL$, $EG = JL$

sections.title: Example: Corresponding Angles in Congruent Triangles
sections.problem: Triangles $EFG$ and $JKL$ are congruent, where $E, F, G$ correspond to $J, K, L$. $\angle E = 45°$ and $\angle F = 20°$. What is the measure of $\angle J$?

sections.title: Same Shape, Different Size
sections.content:
**Similar triangles** have the same angles but different sizes. Their sides are **proportional**.

If $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle XYZ$ with correspondence $A \to X$, $B \to Y$, $C \to Z$:

$$\frac{AB}{XY} = \frac{BC}{YZ} = \frac{AC}{XZ}$$

This ratio is the **scale factor**.

**Conditions for similarity:** AA (two equal angles), SAS, or SSS with proportional sides.

sections.title: Example: Find a Side Using Similarity
sections.problem: Triangle $ABC \sim$ triangle $XYZ$ (A↔X, B↔Y, C↔Z). In $\triangle ABC$: $AB = 170$, $BC = 850$. In $\triangle XYZ$: $YZ = 60$. What is $XY$?

steps.description: Set up the proportion: AB/XY = BC/YZ (corresponding sides are proportional)

sections.tip: Scale factor = 60/850 = 6/85. Then XY = 170 × (6/85) = 12. Always verify which sides correspond.

sections.title: Example: Shadow and Similar Triangles
sections.problem: A 10-foot tree casts a 5-foot shadow. At the same time, another tree casts a 2-foot shadow. How tall is the second tree?

steps.description: The sun creates similar triangles. Set up the proportion: height/shadow = height/shadow

sections.answer: The second tree is $4$ feet tall

sections.title: Angles in a Triangle Sum to 180°
sections.content:
This is the most fundamental triangle rule:
$$\angle A + \angle B + \angle C = 180°$$

**Exterior angle theorem:** An exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two non-adjacent interior angles.

sections.title: Example: Exterior Angle Theorem
sections.problem: In triangle $ABC$, $\angle A = x°$ and $\angle B = y°$. An exterior angle at $C$ is formed. What is its measure?

steps.description: Exterior angle at C = sum of non-adjacent angles A and B

sections.title: Type 5: Overlapping Triangles and Complex Figures
Example: Vertical Angles + Similar Triangles
sections.problem:
[IMAGE PLACEHOLDER: Two triangles sharing vertex R on a line segment PT. Triangle QRP on the left, triangle SUT on the right. Angle QPR is a right angle and angle QRP = x°.]

The triangles share vertex $R$ at the center. Show why $\angle QRP = \angle SRU$.

steps.description: ∠QRP and ∠SRU are vertical angles (formed by two intersecting lines)
Both triangles have a right angle, so they share two angle measures → AA similarity

sections.answer: Vertical angles are equal; the triangles are similar by AA.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: **Parallel + transversal:** corresponding, alternate interior, and alternate exterior angles are equal; co-interior angles are supplementary
**Congruent triangles:** corresponding angles and sides are equal
**Similar triangles:** corresponding angles equal; sides are proportional
**Triangle sum:** all three angles add to $180°$
**Exterior angle:** = sum of the two non-adjacent interior angles
**Vertical angles:** opposite angles at an intersection are equal

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- Confusing which sides correspond in similar triangles (label them carefully)
- Using the wrong angles in the proportion (must use corresponding angles)
- Forgetting the exterior angle theorem — don't try to add up to 360° unnecessarily
- Mixing up supplementary (180°) and complementary (90°)
- Using the wrong scale factor in proportion: always check which triangle's side is in the numerator

sat_tips: Label corresponding vertices clearly before writing a proportion for similar triangles
For parallel line + transversal: draw a Z (alternate) or F (corresponding) shape to identify equal angles
Exterior angle theorem shortcut: exterior angle = sum of the two opposite interior angles
Shadow problems always use similar triangles: height/shadow = height/shadow
